Ventilatory mechanics is the set of phenomena which allow or oppose the renewal of air in the alveoli.
I- Respiratory cycle
Air enters the lungs (inhalation) and leaves them (exhalation) during ventilation.
Inspiration followed by expiration constitutes the respiratory cycle.

It is the result of pressure differences between the atmosphere and the alveoli, differences whose direction is periodically reversed under the effect of the cyclical activity of the respiratory muscles.
The duration of a respiratory cycle is approximately 04 to 05 seconds which corresponds to a respiratory frequency of 12 to 15 cycles/min in humans at rest.
I-Respiratory cycle
A-Respiratory muscles
In calm breathing, inhalation causes the volume of the rib cage to increase and exhalation is a simple return to the base volume.
The contraction of the main inspiratory muscles is responsible for the increase in the volume of the rib cage during inspiration and expiration is due to the relaxation of the inspiratory muscles.
I-Respiratory cycle
A-Respiratory muscles
During calm breathing, expiration is normally a passive phenomenon due to elastic retraction of the lung while inspiration is an active phenomenon requiring energy.
I-Respiratory cycle
A-Respiratory muscles

Deeper Inspiration results from stronger contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles and; of the contraction of the accessory inspiratory muscles located in the neck which pulls the sternum and the first two ribs upwards and increases the volume of the upper part of the rib cage: additional increase in the volume of the rib cage and therefore of the lungs.
I-Respiratory cycle
A-Respiratory muscles

During forced expiration, to deflate the lungs more and faster than during calm ventilation (example of physical exercise) expiration becomes active: contraction of the expiratory muscles (muscles of the abdominal wall and internal intercostal muscles): additional reduction in the volume of the rib cage and lungs.

4-Production of air flow
Since the air flows passively under the effect of a pressure difference, from a high pressure zone to a low pressure zone it is necessary:
-that the Palv ˂ Patm so that it enters the lungs during inspiration;
-that the Palv ˃ Patm so that the air flows out of the lungs during expiration.
The Palv varies depending on the volume of the lungs. The latter is the result of cyclical activity of the respiratory muscles.
The Palv varies in accordance with the Boyle-Mariotte law.

Chapter 2: Ventilatory mechanics 1-Respiratory cycle.
I-Respiratory cycle

In total, the lung volumes can be mobilized thanks to the striated respiratory muscles which develop active contractile forces, thanks to an automatic central nervous command, but also voluntary, since we can modify our breathing within certain limits.
To do this, muscle contraction must oppose the mechanical properties of the lung.
II-Concept of active and passive mechanical systems
1-Introduction
The ventilation system refers to all the structures which ensure ventilation, that is to say the renewal of air. These structures can be schematically grouped into two sets:
one active: the ventilatory muscles;
the other passive
-the airways;
-the lungs;
-the thoracoabdominal wall
II-Concept of active and passive mechanical systems
2-Forces present
The driving force of inspiration is the contraction of the inspiratory muscles which allows the increase of the three diameters of the respiratory system.
These muscles had to fight against resisting forces:
-the elasticity of the thoracopulmonary system which had to be stretched;
-the flow of air in the airways;
-the friction of tissues on themselves;
-the inertia of the system: since the system was at rest.
II-Concept of active and passive mechanical systems
2-Forces present
Normal expiration is the consequence of the elastic and passive return of the respiratory system on itself.

What was previously a resisting force, the elastic retraction of the respiratory system, becomes a driving force, which will fight against the resistance of the airways, which is greater during expiration than during inspiration.
II-Concept of active and passive mechanical systems
3-Relationship driving and resisting forces

The relationship between driving and resisting forces can be expressed by Newton's equation of motion applied to a three-dimensional system, which says that the total pressure applied to the system must be equal to the sum of the products of total elastance times volume, total resistance times flow rate, and inertia times acceleration:
Ptot = Etot × V + Rtot × Q + I×A
II-Concept of active and passive mechanical systems
3-Relationship driving and resisting forces
Ptot = Etot × V + Rtot × Q + I×A
The inertia is negligible, which allows removing the last term and the simplified equation:
Ptot = Etot × V + Rtot × Q

III-Elastic properties of the respiratory system
A-Introduction
In the absence of respiratory movements, that is to say in a static condition, Newton's equation simplifies:
Ptot = Etot × V
This involves studying elastic properties.
III-Elastic properties of the respiratory system
B-Pressure-volume relationship and notion of compliance

Considering Newton's equation in static conditions, the elastance of the respiratory system or its components, the chest wall and the lung, is equal to the ratio of pressure (driving) to volume (mobilized)
Ptot = Etot × V
→ (Etot) = Ptot / V
→ E = P / V
III-Elastic properties of the respiratory system
B-Pressure-volume relationship and notion of compliance
In fact, we do not measure elastance, we prefer its inverse, compliance:
Compliance = 1/elastance: C = 1/E = V/P
In other words, we measure the quantity of air that enters the lung for a change in pressure. Compliance is therefore a measure of the distensibility of the respiratory system.
III-Elastic properties of the respiratory system
B-Pressure-volume relationship and notion of compliance
Respiratory system compliance
The lung-thoracic cage system are elastic structures attached to each other.
Contraction of the inspiratory muscles → stretching of the rib cage → stretching of the lungs.
The stretching or compressure of an elastic structure→ a pressure which tends to return the structure to its initial state (relaxation or rest volume).
III-Elastic properties of the respiratory system
B-Pressure-volume relationship and notion of compliance
Respiratory system compliance
Inside an elastic structure (lung, rib cage, lung rib cage association or other):
-the volume is directly proportional to the pressure difference on either side of the wall (ΔP);
- ΔP is called transmural pressure or wall distension pressure, the more it increases, the more it will distend the structure.
Concept of compliance
An elastic structure can be characterized by the transmural pressure – volume curve.
Biological structures: relaxation volume ≠ 0.
Slope of the ΔV/ΔP curve = compliance.
Compliance characterizes the distensibility of the structure.
The greater the compliance, the more distensible the structure.

It all depends on the transmural pressure considered.
If we want to calculate the pressure-volume curve and the pulmonary compliance we take the transmural pressure which applies to the lung, i.e. Palv- Ppl (transpulmonary pressure).

In a liquid: the water molecules which are at depth are subject to random forces of attraction which cancel each other out.

Example: a little liquid on a flat surface tends to take the shape of a spherical drop for which the air/liquid interface has a minimum surface area.
Surface tension (T) is the surface force of contraction of a liquid thanks to which the air/liquid surface tends to be as small as possible.
In the alveoli, to minimize the air-liquid interface, surface tension tends to collapse the alveoli and cause them to shrivel on themselves. Surface tension is high.

b- Factors of lung elasticity
Thus, lung expansion requires energy to:
-stretch the connective tissuee;
-overcome the surface tension of the layer of water lining the cells.
III-Elastic properties of the respiratory system
2-Surface tension and surfactant

In fact, the surface tension of pure water is so high that if the alveoli were lined only with pure water, lung expansion would require exhaustible muscular effort and the lungs would tend to collapse.

It is therefore essential that type II alveolar cells secrete a substance with detergent properties, called surfactant (surface active agent) which notably reduces the cohesive forces between water molecules on the alveolar surface.
2-Surface tension and surfactant
Surfactant characteristics
1-Pulmonary surfactant is a mixture of phospholipids and proteins
2-It is secreted by type II pneumocytes
3-It lowers the surface tension of the liquid layer on the surface of the alveoli, which increases lung compliance, thus facilitating lung expansion
4-Its most marked effect in small alveoli, which reduces the surface tension of the latter more significantly than in larger alveoli. This stabilizes the alveoli
5-Deep breathing increases its secretion by stretching type II pneumocytes. Its concentration decreases when breathing is shallow
6-It is produced at the end of pregnancy in the fetal lung
IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
A-Introduction
Ventilation in dynamic conditions (when air flow occurs), the activity of the respiratory muscles must overcome:
→lung elasticity;
→the resistance to the passage of air which includes:
-friction of the lung tissuee that is distended;
-airway resistance (VA)
Most important is airway resistance: resistance to the flow of air molecules through the airways.
IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
A-General principles
1-Flow in a bronchial conduction system
The air flows according to:

items: Pressure (ΔP): pressure gradient (Palv –Patm) → air flow; -Flow rate (Q): quantity of air circulating in VA/unit of time; the gas flows from the highest to the lowest pressure;
Resistance(R): difficulty that the air encounters in circulating between 2 points of the VA s/the action of a ΔP.

blocks.text: IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
A-General principles
2-Flow regimes
For a given flow rate, the pressure difference depends on the flow rate and the behavior of the gas.

For low flow rates, the flow of gas in the airways is in a laminar mode. In this case, the flow direction lines are parallel to the walls and Q is directly proportional to ΔP, and R is simply defined by:
R=ΔP/Q
In this case Poiseuille's law allows us to express R for a tube of length (L) and radius (r):
R= 8η L/ π r⁴
We also see that viscosity (η) is the only property of the fluid which contributes to R.
IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
A-General principles
2-Flow regimes

When the flow increases, the flow lines can move away from the wall, particularly at the bronchial divisions with local formation of vortices. If the flow rate increases further, the flow becomes turbulent.
In this case, ΔP between the two ends of the conduit is not proportional to the Q but approximately to its square Q².
IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
A-General principles
2-Flow regimes

The risk of turbulence is higher as the Reynolds number (Re) is greater: Re = ρ× v × d/η, where ρ is the density of the gas, v the average gas flow speed, d the diameter of the bronchus and ηthe viscosity of the gas.
We can also express Re in terms of Q rather than v, in which case the equation of Re will show Q in the numerator and d in the denominator.
IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
A-General principles
2-Flow regimes
In the most proximal airways, the Q is high and d is small, resulting in turbulent flow, particularly at the level of the larynx, whose caliber is reduced.

As the inspired air travels through the respiratory tree, the cumulative cross-section of the airways increases with each generation (see slide no. 59) while at the level of an elementary airway, the flow rate decreases.
The regime therefore becomes laminar, approximately between the 2nd and 4th bronchial generation.
At the alveolar level, gas movements are due to the diffusion of O₂ and CO₂.
IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
B-Distribution of resistance in the airways
Resistance is not uniform throughout the airways.

The flow conditions and the geometry of the respiratory tree, in particular the total section of each generation, mean that the resistance, in the normal subject, is distributed essentially at the level of the proximal airways, including the upper airways.
For example, nasal resistance may represent more than 40% of the total resistance.
IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
B-Distribution of resistance in the airways
On the other hand, bronchoconstriction modifies this distribution:
-in the first bronchial generations, the contraction of smooth muscle has little effect on resistance given the caliber and the presence of cartilage which opposes this contraction;

-on the other hand, the diameter of the small bronchi and bronchioles is small, the cartilage is rare or absent, so there is little or no structural opposition to the contraction of the smooth muscle.
An asthma attack shifts respiratory resistance toward these airways.
IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
B-Distribution of resistance in the airways
The resistance to gas passage in the airways is inversely proportional to the total cross-sectional area.
In adults, at the level of the trachea and main bronchi, the total cross-sectional area is small (2 or 3 cm²) and the resistance is high.
The peripheral airways have lower resistance because the total surface area is approximately 500 times greater.
IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
B-Distribution of resistance in the airways
Examples
The anatomical arrangement makes the nose effective as an air conditioning system and also creates great resistance to flow.

During quiet ventilation, a normal subject tolerates the additional work that nasal ventilation offers. However, in the event of muscular exercise, ventilation can become oral in order to reduce the work required by hyperventilation.
IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
B-Distribution of resistance in the airways
Examples
The pharynx is characterized by the wealth of striated muscles and their innervation.
During inspiration, the diaphragm generates negative pressure in the airways, which tends to collapse the pharynx. The muscles of the pharynx, by stiffening the pharyngeal wall, prevent obstruction.
However, during sleep, negative pressure can lead to pharyngeal collapse because muscle tone decreases and obstructive apnea can result.
IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
C-Factors determining airway resistance
1-Lung volume
Due to pulmonary architecture (mechanical coupling between the airways and the pulmonary parenchyma), the diameter of the bronchi increases with lung volume.
Airway resistance decreases as lung volume increases.

blocks.text: IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system
C-Factors determining airway resistance
2-Bronchial smooth muscle
Contraction of the smooth muscle of the bronchial walls is controlled by nervous and humoral mechanisms.
Nervous control involves
afferent pathways carried by the vagus nerve, which originate from receptors sensitive to:
- stretching of the airway wall;
- irritation of the bronchial epithelium by mechanical or chemical stimuli;
-irritation of the pulmonary interstitium;
central nuclei located in the medulla oblongata;
motor efferent pathways are
-either cholinergic (their activation causes bronchoconstriction via muscarinic receptors),
-either adrenergic (their activation causes bronchodilation via β2-adrenergic receptors),
-either non-adrenergic, non-cholinergic (NANC).

pages.title: IV-Resistive properties of the respiratory system

blocks.text: C-Factors determining airway resistance
2-Bronchial smooth muscle
Humoral mechanisms (endocrine or paracrine): example histamine and other inflammatory substances secreted during an acute asthma attack → bronchoconstriction
Local accumulations of mucus, infectious materials and tumors obstructing the airways constitute major sources of resistance in respiratory diseases.

blocks.text: VI-Dead space and ventilation differences
Pulmonary ventilation or minute ventilation or air flow is the volume of air inspired and expired in one minute:
Pulmonary ventilation = tidal volume (VT)
(ml/min) (ml) (cycles/min)
Respiratory frequency = number of cycles per minute which is on average 12 to 16 cycles/min in a resting adult.
Anatomical dead space

Not all of the inspired air reaches the alveoli; a part remains in the air conduction pathways which do not participate in gas exchange. This volume of air is 150 ml in normal adults; this is the anatomical dead space.
VI-Dead space and ventilation differences
Alveolar dead space

items: Atmospheric air enters the alveoli and participates in the exchange of O2 and CO2 with the blood in the pulmonary capillaries.

However, certain ventilated alveoli are not perfused by blood and do not participate in gas exchange and constitute the alveolar dead space. The sum of the two dead spaces (anatomical and alveolar) corresponds to the physiological or total dead space.

blocks.text: Alveolar ventilation is the volume of air exchanged per minute between the alveoli and the atmosphere:
Alveolar ventilation =
(tidal volume – volume of physiological dead space)
